title: Immunisation in pregnancy
blurb: Time pertussis, RSV and flu vaccines correctly in every pregnancy, and explain why live vaccines usually wait until after the birth.
question: Precious is 25 weeks pregnant with her first baby in October. She has not had any vaccines in this pregnancy and asks which she needs and when. What should the midwife advise?

teach.h: Vaccinating the woman protects the baby
teach.body: Three vaccines are offered in pregnancy in the UK: pertussis (whooping cough) and RSV in every pregnancy, and inactivated flu to every pregnant woman during the flu season. The woman makes antibodies, and these cross the placenta, so the baby is born with protection before it can be vaccinated itself. In plain English: the woman's vaccine is the baby's first shield. Flu vaccine also protects the woman, who is more likely than non-pregnant women to have serious flu complications.
teach.cite: UKHSA Green Book ch 24, 27a, 19 (schedule from 1 Sept 2026)

items.label: Pertussis can be given from here
RSV can be given up to delivery

teach.caption: Pertussis given after 32 weeks still protects the woman and lowers the baby's exposure, but gives less passive protection.

rows.label: Examples
values: MMR, BCG, yellow fever, oral typhoid

teach.caption: There is no evidence that any live vaccine causes birth defects; occasionally one is given if the infection risk is greater (NHS).

teach.body: Maternal antibody levels fall after birth, so protection does not carry over to the next baby. Pertussis is a single 0.5 mL dose in every pregnancy; RSV vaccine is offered in every pregnancy; flu is offered each season. The aim is peak antibody transfer before birth, which is why RSV is best given in week 28 or soon after and pertussis ideally before 32 weeks.

teach.h: A woman asks: can I have this vaccine now?

children.label: Usually postpone
children.sub: Until after the birth; seek advice

teach.body: Precious is past 16 weeks and has not had pertussis, so the midwife offers it now: before 32 weeks gives her baby the best protection. It is October, so inactivated flu is offered too, as it can be given at any stage. RSV cannot be given yet; the midwife books it for her 28-week appointment and explains it protects the baby from severe RSV in the first months. Each decision is recorded in her notes.

teach.text: Do not swap the start points: pertussis from 16 weeks, RSV from 28 weeks. And 'flu vaccine' in pregnancy means the injected inactivated vaccine, which the Green Book prefers in pregnancy: the live nasal spray (LAIV) is the children's programme vaccine, not the one offered to pregnant women.

items: Pertussis: one dose every pregnancy, from 16 weeks, usually around 20, ideally before 32; later still helps.
RSV (Abrysvo): every pregnancy, from 28 weeks, ideally that week; can be given until delivery.
Flu: inactivated injection at any stage of pregnancy; the live nasal spray is the children's vaccine, not the one offered in pregnancy.
Live vaccines such as MMR usually wait until after the birth.
Babies born under 32 weeks are offered a long-acting RSV monoclonal antibody.

summary: You can now time pertussis, RSV and flu vaccination for any gestation, explain that each is repeated in every pregnancy, and advise that live vaccines usually wait until after the birth. You can also explain how maternal antibodies protect the newborn.

A.q: From which gestation can the pertussis (whooping cough) vaccine first be given in pregnancy?
A.why: Green Book ch 24: the pertussis vaccine can be given from 16 weeks, and is usually given around the 20-week anomaly scan.

whyNot.0: 12 weeks is earlier than the recommended start of 16 weeks.
whyNot.2: 20 weeks is when it is usually given, but it can be given from 16.
whyNot.3: 28 weeks is the start point for the RSV vaccine.

A.q: A woman at her 25-week appointment asks when she can have the RSV vaccine. What is the correct answer?
A.why: Green Book ch 27a: Abrysvo is offered from 28 weeks in every pregnancy, ideally in week 28 or soon after.

whyNot.0: 16 weeks is the pertussis start point.
whyNot.1: 24 weeks is earlier than the RSV programme start of 28 weeks.
whyNot.3: 32 weeks is the ideal pertussis deadline, not the RSV start.

A.q: In October, a woman who is 9 weeks pregnant asks whether she should wait before having the flu vaccine. What is the best advice?
options: Have the nasal spray vaccine instead
A.why: Green Book ch 19: inactivated flu vaccine is offered at any stage of pregnancy. Pregnant women are at higher risk of flu complications.

whyNot.0: There is no need to wait: any trimester is suitable.
whyNot.1: The nasal spray (LAIV) is the children's live vaccine; the Green Book prefers inactivated vaccine in pregnancy.
whyNot.2: Waiting leaves her and her baby unprotected through the flu season.

B.q: Joanna is 20 weeks pregnant. She had the pertussis vaccine in her last pregnancy, 14 months ago. What should the midwife advise?
options: Offer it again: one dose in every pregnancy
It is not needed while last year's dose lasts
A half dose is enough as a booster
Check her antibody levels before offering it
B.why: Green Book ch 24: a single dose is offered in every pregnancy, because antibody levels fall and each baby needs fresh passive protection.

whyNot.1: Protection for the new baby depends on high antibody levels in this pregnancy.
whyNot.2: The dose is the full 0.5 mL in each pregnancy.
whyNot.3: Antibody testing is not part of the programme; the vaccine is simply offered.

B.q: Mei is 34 weeks pregnant and missed her pertussis vaccine. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: It is too late to be useful after 32 weeks
Offer it now: it still protects her and the baby
Give the baby a dose at birth instead
Offer it at her six-week postnatal check
B.why: Green Book ch 24: ideally before 32 weeks, but it can still be given later; it protects the woman and so reduces the baby's exposure.

whyNot.0: Later vaccination still has value, though passive protection is lower.
whyNot.2: Babies start their own pertussis vaccines at 8 weeks, not at birth.
whyNot.3: Waiting until after the birth loses the chance of any antenatal protection.

B.q: Fatima, 18 weeks pregnant, is unsure whether she had MMR as a child and asks for it now. What should the midwife explain?
options: Have it now, as rubella in pregnancy harms the baby
Have it after 28 weeks, once organs have formed
MMR is live, so it usually waits until after birth
Have it with her pertussis vaccine at 20 weeks
B.why: MMR is a live vaccine; women are usually advised to wait until after the birth because of a theoretical risk of fetal infection (NHS).

whyNot.0: Rubella is harmful, but a live vaccine is usually not given in pregnancy.
whyNot.1: Gestation does not make a live vaccine routine in pregnancy.
whyNot.3: Pertussis is inactivated; MMR is live and usually postponed.

C.q: Ruth declined the RSV vaccine in pregnancy. Her baby is born at 29 weeks during the RSV season. What is the baby likely to be offered?
options: The Abrysvo vaccine on day one
C.why: Green Book ch 27a (June 2026): very or extremely preterm infants (under 32 weeks) are offered a long-acting monoclonal antibody (nirsevimab or clesrovimab).

whyNot.0: Abrysvo is given to the pregnant woman, not to the newborn.
whyNot.2: There is no infant RSV vaccine at 8 weeks; preterm babies get antibody protection.
whyNot.3: Vaccinating the mother after birth gives the baby no transplacental antibodies.

C.q: Bisi is 24 weeks pregnant in November and had her pertussis vaccine at 20 weeks. She has not had flu or RSV vaccines. Which plan is correct?
options: Flu after 28 weeks; RSV from 32 weeks
RSV now; flu after the birth
Flu and RSV now, at the same visit
C.why: Inactivated flu can be given at any stage, so give it now in the flu season. RSV is offered from 28 weeks, ideally in week 28.

whyNot.0: Flu should not wait, and RSV starts at 28, not 32, weeks.
whyNot.1: RSV cannot be given before 28 weeks, and flu should not wait until after birth.
whyNot.3: At 24 weeks she is too early for the RSV vaccine.

C.q: A woman asks why she should have the whooping cough vaccine herself rather than the baby having it straight after birth. Which explanation is accurate?
options: The vaccine germ passes to the baby and immunises it
Breast milk carries the vaccine to the baby after birth
It triggers the baby's own immune response in the womb
Her antibodies cross the placenta and protect the newborn
C.why: Maternal vaccination produces antibodies that cross the placenta, protecting the baby until its own pertussis vaccines begin at 8 weeks.

whyNot.0: The pertussis vaccine is inactivated; nothing live passes to the baby.
whyNot.1: The protection described is transplacental antibody, given before birth.
whyNot.2: The baby receives the woman's ready-made antibodies; it is not itself immunised.

reteach.title: Sixteen, twenty-eight, any
reteach.question: If you remember three numbers, can you time every pregnancy vaccine?

blocks.body: Pertussis starts at 16 weeks and is best done before 32. RSV starts at 28 weeks and is best done that week. Flu has no start point: any stage of pregnancy, in season. Each is repeated in every pregnancy. Live vaccines such as MMR usually wait until after the birth.

blocks.text: Pertussis after 32 weeks is not 'too late': it still protects the woman and lowers the baby's exposure.

explain.body: A single 0.5 mL dose in every pregnancy, from 16 weeks, usually around 20 weeks, ideally before 32 weeks for best passive protection. It can still be given later.

test.q: Before which gestation is pertussis vaccine ideally given for the best protection of the baby?
test.why: Green Book ch 24: ideally before 32 weeks for best passive protection.

whyNot.0: 24 weeks is within the window, but the ideal deadline is 32 weeks.
whyNot.1: 28 weeks is the RSV start point.
whyNot.3: 36 weeks is later than the ideal; protection for the baby is lower.

explain.body: Abrysvo is offered from 28 weeks in every pregnancy, ideally in week 28 or soon after, and can be given up to delivery (less passive protection late). Babies born under 32 weeks are offered a long-acting monoclonal antibody.

test.q: When is the RSV vaccine ideally given in pregnancy?
test.why: Green Book ch 27a: from 28 weeks, ideally in week 28 or soon after.

whyNot.0: 16 weeks is the earliest pertussis gestation.
whyNot.1: 20 weeks is the usual pertussis time.
whyNot.2: It can be given at 36 weeks, but passive protection is lower than at 28.

explain.body: The inactivated (injected) flu vaccine is offered at any stage of pregnancy during the flu season. The Green Book prefers inactivated vaccine in pregnancy; the live attenuated nasal spray (LAIV) is used in the children's programme.

test.q: Which flu vaccine is offered to a woman who is 7 weeks pregnant?
test.why: Green Book ch 19: inactivated flu vaccine is given at any stage of pregnancy.

whyNot.1: The nasal spray (LAIV) is the children's live vaccine; inactivated vaccine is preferred in pregnancy.
whyNot.2: There is no need to wait for the second trimester.
whyNot.3: Waiting until after birth leaves her unprotected during pregnancy.

explain.body: Live vaccines (MMR, BCG, yellow fever, oral typhoid) are usually postponed until after the birth because of a theoretical risk of fetal infection, though none has been shown to cause birth defects.

test.q: Which of these vaccines is usually postponed until after the birth?
test.why: MMR is a live vaccine, so it is usually given after the birth.

whyNot.0: Pertussis vaccine is recommended in pregnancy.
whyNot.2: Injected flu vaccine is inactivated and recommended at any stage.
